question: Give your narrative strong internal structure that regulates pace and builds dramatic tension.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Strong internal structure would regulate pace and create dramatic tension.

question: Turn the sources of your true story into characters and its topics into scenes.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Instead of sources, it would have characters. Instead of topics, it would have scenes.

question: Keep your account scrupulously accurate while pushing toward truths beyond the reach of a routine report.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It would be scrupulously accurate, but it would reveal truths beyond the reach of an ordinary news report.

question: Match your form to your material: when a subject is best served by simple informational writing, make the key point quickly instead of building a narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But experience has taught me that most subjects are best suited to simple informational writing that makes the key point quickly.

question: Learn enough story theory to recognize when you are forcing narrative onto material that does not call for it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Another is learning enough about story theory to avoid the fatal error of forcing narrative onto inappropriate material.

question: When your audience needs a key point quickly, skip the long narrative windup and lead with it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: if your neighbors want to know if their school will be closed, you’d be foolish to begin a report on the critical school board meeting with a long narrative windup.

question: Master a wide variety of narrative forms rather than relying on a single one.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Mastering a wide variety of narrative forms is one key to success.

question: Do not let lack of experience keep you from narrative: grasp a few core principles, find an appropriate story structure, and draft from there.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: don’t let lack of experience intimidate you. Time and again I’ve seen writers with absolutely no narrative experience grasp a few core principles, ﬁ nd appropriate story structures, and draft dramatic tales that moved readers.

question: Ground your story in specific real-world decisions, applying abstract story principles to the actual material at hand.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Good narrative comes from speciﬁc real- world decisions made by writers and editors who not only understand the abstract principles of story, but also know how to apply them in the real world.

question: Care more about how well your story is told than about where it appears.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: where a story appeared is far less important than how well it was told.

question: Use immersion reporting as a core technique for your nonfiction narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As Ted Conover demonstrated, both ethnography and nonﬁ ction narrative share immersion reporting as a core technique.

question: Show how one action leads to another so your story makes sense of a confusing world.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Story makes sense out of a confusing universe by showing us how one action leads to another.

question: Decide deliberately what to include in your narrative and what to leave out.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Help with their reporting, help with their selection of scenes, help with their descriptions of characters, and help with their choices about what to include and what to leave out.
